subject: Urology
title: Urological Emergencies
subtitle: Acute retention, scrotal and penile emergencies, necrotizing infection and urotrauma
sourceNote: Built only from the uploaded Urological emergencies7 lecture. The bank preserves the lecture definitions, timing, investigations and management statements without adding external guideline details.

cases.title: Acute Urinary Retention
cases.scenario: A 72-year-old man develops sudden complete inability to pass urine with severe lower abdominal pain and a tense distended bladder. He has a previous history of lower urinary tract symptoms.
cases.ar: رجل 72 سنة حصل له sudden complete inability to urinate مع severe suprapubic pain وdistended bladder.
questions: What is the diagnosis?
List the causes mentioned in the lecture.
What is the immediate first-line treatment?
What should be done after stabilization?
answer: Diagnosis: acute urinary retention.
Causes mentioned: BPH, urethral stricture, medications and neurological disorders.
Immediate bladder catheterization to decompress the bladder using an indwelling Foley catheter or a suprapubic catheter.
After stabilization, identify and treat the underlying cause to prevent recurrence.
cases.trap: Do not delay bladder decompression while investigating the cause.
cases.memory: Acute retention = sudden inability + painful bladder → immediate catheterization.

cases.title: Adolescent with Sudden Scrotal Pain
cases.scenario: A 16-year-old boy presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, nausea and vomiting. The affected testis is high-riding.
cases.ar: ولد 16 سنة عنده sudden severe scrotal pain مع swelling وvomiting والخصية high-riding.
questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?
State the underlying mechanism and important risk factor.
How is the diagnosis made?
Outline urgent management and the time window.
What is the role of manual detorsion?
answer: Diagnosis: testicular torsion.
Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off testicular blood supply. A bell-clapper deformity is an important risk factor; it is common in adolescents during rapid growth.
Diagnosis is primarily clinical by physical examination; Doppler ultrasound may confirm reduced blood flow.
Urgent surgical detorsion and orchiopexy should be performed within 6 hours to maximize testicular salvage. After 24 hours the testis can rarely be saved.
Manual detorsion may be attempted but must not delay surgery.
cases.trap: Doppler confirmation must not delay urgent surgical intervention.
cases.memory: Torsion: sudden pain + high testis → surgery within 6 hours.

cases.title: Painful Erection for More Than 4 Hours
cases.scenario: A man presents with a prolonged painful erection lasting 6 hours and unrelated to sexual arousal.
cases.ar: مريض عنده painful erection مستمر 6 ساعات ومش مرتبط بـsexual arousal.
questions: Define the condition.
What type is most likely?
Outline the treatment stated in the lecture.
How does the other major type differ in urgency and management?
answer: Priapism is a prolonged painful erection lasting more than 4 hours and unrelated to sexual arousal.
The painful emergency pattern is ischemic (low-flow) priapism.
Aspirate blood from the corpora cavernosa, then inject a sympathomimetic agent such as phenylephrine directly into the corpora.
Non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism is usually less urgent; urological consultation, observation and ice packs may be sufficient.
cases.trap: Do not treat ischemic and non-ischemic priapism as equally urgent.
cases.memory: Ischemic = painful low flow → aspirate then intracavernosal phenylephrine.

cases.title: High-Flow Priapism
cases.scenario: A patient has a prolonged erection after trauma but is otherwise stable, and the urologist considers a high-flow form.
cases.ar: مريض بعد trauma عنده prolonged erection ويُشتبه في high-flow priapism.
questions: Classify priapism into its two main types.
Which type is usually less urgent?
State the management options mentioned for this type.
State the emergency treatment of the low-flow type.
answer: Types: ischemic (low-flow) and non-ischemic (high-flow).
Non-ischemic high-flow priapism is usually less urgent.
Urological consultation; observation and ice packs may be sufficient.
Low-flow ischemic priapism: aspiration from the corpora cavernosa followed by intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection such as phenylephrine.
cases.trap: “Less urgent” does not mean no urological assessment.
cases.memory: High flow: consult, observe, ice; low flow: aspirate + phenylephrine.

cases.title: Snap, Detumescence and Eggplant Deformity
cases.scenario: During vigorous intercourse, a man hears an audible crack followed by immediate loss of erection, severe pain, swelling and dark-purple penile bruising.
cases.ar: أثناء intercourse سمع crack وبعدها immediate detumescence مع pain وeggplant deformity.
questions: What is the diagnosis and injured structure?
List the characteristic symptoms and signs.
What finding suggests associated urethral injury?
What is the standard treatment?
List complications of delayed treatment.
answer: Diagnosis: penile fracture — traumatic rupture of the tunica albuginea of the erect penis.
Audible snap/crack, rapid detumescence, marked pain and swelling, and eggplant deformity from dark-purple hematoma.
Blood at the penile tip/urethral bleeding suggests urethral injury.
Immediate surgical exploration and repair of the tunica albuginea tear.
Delayed complications: penile curvature (Peyronie disease), erectile dysfunction and painful intercourse.
cases.trap: The classic sequence is crack → immediate detumescence → swelling/eggplant deformity.
cases.memory: Penile fracture = tunica tear + snap + detumescence → immediate repair.

cases.title: Painful Swollen Glans after Retraction
cases.scenario: A retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans. The glans is swollen and very painful.
cases.ar: الـprepuce اتسحب للخلف ومش قادر يرجع مكانه مع swollen painful glans.
questions: What is the diagnosis?
Differentiate it from phimosis.
Why is it a true emergency?
Outline management if manual repositioning fails.
answer: Diagnosis: paraphimosis.
Phimosis: inability to retract the prepuce behind the glans. Paraphimosis: the prepuce is retracted and cannot return to its original position.
Delay may cause gangrene of the glans.
Attempt manual preputial repositioning; if this fails, urgent dorsal slit incision may relieve the constricting ring.
cases.trap: Do not confuse inability to retract (phimosis) with inability to return a retracted foreskin (paraphimosis).
cases.memory: Paraphimosis = trapped retracted foreskin → reduce; dorsal slit if failed.

cases.title: Rapidly Progressive Perineal Sepsis
cases.scenario: A diabetic-looking septic patient has severe perineal and scrotal pain, swelling, erythema and crepitus with fever and hypotension.
cases.ar: مريض septic عنده severe perineal/scrotal pain مع swelling وerythema وcrepitus وhypotension.
questions: What is the diagnosis and definition?
List the local and systemic features.
State the three urgent management pillars.
Why must treatment be immediate?
answer: Diagnosis: Fournier's gangrene — rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, scrotum and genitalia.
Local features: severe pain, swelling, erythema and crepitus. Systemic features include fever and hypotension.

Immediate aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram-positive, gram-negative and anaerobic organisms; intensive supportive care with fluid resuscitation and septic-shock management.
Rapid progression can produce life-threatening sepsis; immediate treatment is critical.
cases.trap: Antibiotics alone are not sufficient; aggressive surgical debridement is critical.
cases.memory: Fournier = debride now + broad IV antibiotics + resuscitate.

cases.title: Stable Blunt Renal Trauma
cases.scenario: After a road-traffic accident, a hemodynamically stable patient has flank pain, ecchymosis and haematuria.
cases.ar: بعد blunt trauma مريض stable عنده flank pain وecchymosis وhaematuria.
questions: What organ injury is suspected?
State the common mechanism and clinical features.
What is the primary diagnostic investigation?
Outline management for most cases.
List early and delayed complications.
answer: Renal trauma.
Most renal trauma follows blunt impact (about 80–90%); features include haematuria, abdominal or flank pain, ecchymosis and shock.
CT scan with angiography to define the injury and grade it on the AAST scale.
Most stable cases receive non-operative management with bed rest, hydration and monitoring.
Early: persistent bleeding, infection and urine leakage. Delayed: hypertension and urinoma.
cases.trap: Haematuria is common, but management is driven by the overall injury and hemodynamic status.
cases.memory: Stable renal trauma → CT angiography → usually observe.

cases.title: Renal Trauma with Active Bleeding
cases.scenario: CT angiography after renal trauma demonstrates active bleeding. The patient is being assessed for a minimally invasive haemostatic procedure.
cases.ar: CT angiography بعد renal trauma يظهر active bleeding.
questions: Which treatment is specifically mentioned for active bleeding?
When is surgical repair/renorrhaphy reserved?
Summarize AAST grades 1–5 from the lecture chart.
answer: Angioembolization is used for active bleeding.
Surgical repair (renorrhaphy) is reserved for severe injury; unstable patients may require operative management.

AAST chart: Grade 1 contusion or non-expanding subcapsular hematoma, no laceration. Grade 2 non-expanding perirenal hematoma or cortical laceration under 1 cm without urinary extravasation. Grade 3 cortical laceration over 1 cm without urinary extravasation. Grade 4 laceration through the corticomedullary junction into the collecting system or segmental vascular injury with contained hematoma/partial laceration/thrombosis. Grade 5 shattered kidney or renal-pedicle avulsion.
cases.trap: Active bleeding does not automatically mean nephrectomy; the lecture highlights angioembolization.
cases.memory: Active bleed → angioembolize; severe/unstable injury → surgery.

cases.title: Delayed Ureteral Injury after Pelvic Surgery
cases.scenario: Several days after hysterectomy, a patient develops persistent flank pain, fever, ileus and urine leakage.
cases.ar: بعد hysterectomy ظهرت delayed flank pain وfever وileus وurine leakage.
questions: What injury should be suspected and what is its commonest cause?
Why is the diagnosis often delayed?
List the diagnostic tests mentioned.
Outline management of minor and significant injury.
List complications of missed injury.
answer: Suspect ureteral trauma; iatrogenic injury is the commonest cause, especially during gynecologic surgery such as hysterectomy, as well as urological and colorectal surgery.
Symptoms are often delayed and many injuries are diagnosed postoperatively (70–80% in the lecture).
CT urography with contrast and delayed images, intravenous pyelogram, or retrograde pyelogram.

Minor injury: conservative management with JJ stent. Significant injury: early repair by endoscopic stenting, ureteroureterostomy or ureteroneocystostomy. Percutaneous nephrostomy may provide urinary diversion.
Urinoma, renal failure, stricture, fistula and sepsis.
cases.trap: A normal early postoperative course does not exclude ureteral injury; presentation may be delayed.
cases.memory: Post-op flank pain + urine leak → think ureter; delayed CT urography.

cases.title: Pelvic Fracture with Extraperitoneal Bladder Injury
cases.scenario: A patient with a pelvic fracture develops gross haematuria, suprapubic pain and inability to void. Imaging shows urine leaking into pelvic tissues.
cases.ar: مريض pelvic fracture عنده gross haematuria وsuprapubic pain، والبول متسرب للـpelvic tissues.
questions: What type of bladder injury is present?
List common clinical features.
What is the standard diagnostic study?
State the usual treatment and duration.
answer: Extraperitoneal bladder injury.
Gross haematuria, suprapubic pain, inability to urinate or weak/strained stream, abdominal tenderness and distention.
CT cystogram or conventional X-ray cystography.
Usually non-operative urinary-catheter drainage for about 10–14 days to allow healing.
cases.trap: Extraperitoneal injury is strongly linked to pelvic fracture and is usually treated with catheter drainage.
cases.memory: EP bladder rupture → pelvic tissues → catheter 10–14 days.

cases.title: Full Bladder Rupture into the Peritoneum
cases.scenario: After a blow to a distended bladder, cystography shows contrast entering the abdominal cavity from a tear at the bladder dome.
cases.ar: ضربة على full bladder سببت dome rupture وتسرب للـperitoneal cavity.
questions: What type of rupture is this?
How does it differ anatomically from extraperitoneal rupture?
What is the diagnostic test?
What is the treatment?
List complications if untreated.
answer: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture.
Intraperitoneal: urine leaks into the abdominal cavity, usually from the dome of a full bladder. Extraperitoneal: urine leaks into pelvic tissues and is often associated with pelvic fractures.
CT cystogram or conventional cystography.
Almost always surgical repair, laparoscopic or open.
Infection, abscess, persistent leakage and long-term kidney dysfunction.
cases.trap: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is not managed like an uncomplicated extraperitoneal tear.
cases.memory: IP bladder rupture = dome + peritoneal urine → surgical repair.

cases.title: Pelvic Fracture with Blood at the Meatus
cases.scenario: After high-impact pelvic trauma, a man has blood at the urethral meatus, urinary retention, perineal ecchymosis and a floating prostate on examination.
cases.ar: بعد pelvic fracture ظهر blood at meatus وretention وperineal ecchymosis وfloating prostate.
questions: What injury is most likely?
Differentiate posterior from anterior urethral injury by mechanism.
What is the standard imaging test and expected finding?
What is the preferred initial urinary diversion?
Outline definitive management and complications.
answer: Posterior urethral injury, often associated with pelvic fracture.
Posterior injuries: pelvic fractures from high-impact accidents. Anterior injuries: straddle injury or direct penile trauma.
Retrograde urethrogram (RGU), often showing contrast extravasation.
Initial suprapubic tube (SPT) insertion is often preferred for urinary diversion.
Partial tears may be managed conservatively; complete injuries require urethroplasty, often delayed 3–6 months. Complications: urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.
cases.trap: Blood at the meatus after pelvic trauma should trigger urethral evaluation before routine urethral instrumentation.
cases.memory: Pelvic fracture + blood at meatus → RGU → SPT.

cases.title: Straddle Injury to the Anterior Urethra
cases.scenario: A cyclist falls astride a hard bar and develops perineal bruising, blood at the meatus and inability to void.
cases.ar: وقع على bicycle bar وعنده perineal bruising وblood at meatus وretention.
questions: Which part of the urethra is commonly injured?
State the mechanism of anterior versus posterior urethral trauma.
What is the standard investigation?
State initial and later management.
answer: This mechanism commonly injures the anterior urethra.
Anterior: straddle injury or direct penile trauma. Posterior: pelvic fracture after high-impact trauma.
Retrograde urethrogram showing the site and possible contrast extravasation.
Initial suprapubic diversion is often preferred. Partial tears may be treated conservatively; complete injuries may need delayed urethroplasty after 3–6 months.
cases.trap: Straddle injury points to anterior urethral trauma, not the classic posterior pelvic-fracture injury.

cases.title: Blunt Scrotal Trauma with Suspected Testicular Rupture
cases.scenario: After a sports injury, a man has intense scrotal pain, nausea, bruising and marked swelling that makes examination difficult. Doppler ultrasound suggests loss of tunica integrity.
cases.ar: بعد sports injury عنده severe scrotal pain وswelling، والـDoppler يشك في rupture.
questions: What is the best imaging modality?
List the types of scrotal/testicular injury in the lecture.
Define testicular rupture and fracture.
When is surgical exploration required?
List long-term complications.
answer: High-resolution scrotal ultrasound with Doppler is the gold standard to assess testicular integrity and blood flow.
Testicular rupture, testicular fracture, intratesticular or extratesticular hematoma, dislocation and torsion.
Rupture: tear of the tunica albuginea with extrusion of tubules. Fracture: disruption of testicular parenchyma without complete tunica-albuginea tear.
Explore for suspected rupture, significant hematocele, persistent severe symptoms, and penetrating injury.
Testicular atrophy, chronic pain, infertility, psychological impact; hematomas may become infected.
cases.trap: Severe swelling can obscure examination; Doppler imaging becomes essential.
cases.memory: Scrotal trauma + suspected rupture → Doppler → urgent exploration.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate the common non-traumatic urological emergencies listed in the lecture.
a: Acute urinary retention.
Testicular torsion.
Priapism.
Penile fracture.
Paraphimosis.
Fournier's gangrene.

coreShorts.q: Define acute urinary retention and list its causes in the lecture.
a: Sudden inability to urinate with severe lower abdominal pain and discomfort.
Causes: BPH, urethral stricture, medications and neurological disorders.

coreShorts.q: Outline immediate and subsequent management of acute urinary retention.
a: Immediate bladder catheterization to decompress the bladder: Foley or suprapubic catheter.
After stabilization, identify and treat the underlying cause to prevent recurrence.

coreShorts.q: Describe the clinical presentation of testicular torsion.
a: Sudden severe scrotal pain and swelling.
Nausea and vomiting may occur.
The affected testis may be higher than usual.

coreShorts.q: State the diagnosis and management principles of testicular torsion.
a: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; Doppler ultrasound may confirm reduced blood flow.
Urgent surgical detorsion and orchiopexy within 6 hours.
After 24 hours salvage is rare.
Manual detorsion may be attempted but must not delay surgery.

coreShorts.q: State the important risk factors for testicular torsion.
a: Bell-clapper deformity allows the testis to hang freely and twist.
Most common in teenagers during rapid growth, although it may occur at any age.

coreShorts.q: Define priapism and classify it.
a: A prolonged painful erection lasting more than 4 hours and unrelated to sexual arousal.
Types: ischemic low-flow and non-ischemic high-flow.

coreShorts.q: Compare management of ischemic and non-ischemic priapism.
a: Ischemic: aspirate blood from the corpora cavernosa, then inject intracavernosal sympathomimetic such as phenylephrine.
Non-ischemic: usually less urgent; urological consultation, observation and ice packs may be sufficient.

coreShorts.q: Define penile fracture and enumerate its classical features.
a: Traumatic rupture of the tunica albuginea of an erect penis.
Audible snap/crack.
Rapid detumescence.
Pain and rapid swelling.
Eggplant deformity from dark-purple hematoma.
Urethral bleeding if the urethra is injured.

coreShorts.q: State treatment and complications of delayed penile-fracture management.
a: Immediate surgical exploration and repair of the tunica-albuginea tear.
Delayed complications: penile curvature/Peyronie disease, erectile dysfunction and painful intercourse.

coreShorts.q: Differentiate phimosis and paraphimosis.
a: Phimosis: inability to retract the prepuce behind the glans.
Paraphimosis: retracted prepuce cannot return to its original position, causing painful glans swelling.

coreShorts.q: Why is paraphimosis a true emergency and how is it managed?
a: Delay may lead to gangrene of the glans.
Attempt manual preputial repositioning.
If manual reduction fails, urgent dorsal-slit incision may be required.

coreShorts.q: Define Fournier's gangrene and state its presentation.
a: Rapidly progressing necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, scrotum and genitalia.
Severe pain, swelling, erythema and crepitus.
Systemic infection may produce fever and hypotension.

coreShorts.q: Outline the emergency management of Fournier's gangrene.
a: Immediate aggressive surgical debridement.
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram-positive, gram-negative and anaerobic organisms.
ICU supportive care, fluid resuscitation and septic-shock management.

coreShorts.q: Classify traumatic urological emergencies and mechanisms.
a: Organs: renal, ureteral, bladder, urethral and scrotal trauma.
Mechanism: blunt or penetrating.
Penetrating projectiles: high/medium velocity such as rifle/handgun bullets, or low velocity such as knife stab.

coreShorts.q: Describe renal-trauma mechanism, symptoms and diagnosis.
a: Most injuries are blunt, about 80–90%, from accidents or falls; penetrating injuries include gunshots.
Symptoms: haematuria, abdominal or flank pain, ecchymosis and shock.
Diagnosis: CT scan with angiography and AAST grading.

coreShorts.q: Summarize the AAST renal injury grades shown in the lecture.
a: Grade 1: contusion or non-expanding subcapsular hematoma, no laceration.
Grade 2: non-expanding perirenal hematoma or cortical laceration <1 cm without urinary extravasation.
Grade 3: cortical laceration >1 cm without urinary extravasation.
Grade 4: laceration into collecting system or segmental vascular injury with contained hematoma/partial laceration/thrombosis.
Grade 5: shattered kidney or renal-pedicle avulsion.

coreShorts.q: Outline treatment and complications of renal trauma.
a: Most cases: non-operative bed rest, hydration and monitoring.
Active bleeding: angioembolization.
Severe injury: surgical repair/renorrhaphy.
Early complications: persistent bleeding, infection and urine leakage.
Delayed: hypertension and urinoma.

coreShorts.q: State causes of ureteral trauma.
a: Iatrogenic is most common: gynecologic surgery especially hysterectomy, urological surgery and colorectal surgery.
External trauma: high-speed accidents, falls and penetrating wounds near L2–L3.

coreShorts.q: Describe presentation and diagnosis of ureteral trauma.
a: Presentation is often delayed: persistent abdominal/flank pain, fever, haematuria, ileus and urine leakage.
Many are diagnosed postoperatively, 70–80% in the lecture.
Tests: CT urography with contrast and delayed imaging, IVP or retrograde pyelogram.

coreShorts.q: Outline management and complications of ureteral trauma.
a: Minor injury: conservative treatment/JJ stent.
Significant injury: early repair by endoscopic stenting, ureteroureterostomy or ureteroneocystostomy.
Percutaneous nephrostomy for diversion.
Complications: urinoma, renal failure, stricture, fistula and sepsis.

coreShorts.q: Classify bladder injury and describe each type.
a: Extraperitoneal: urine into pelvic tissues; often associated with pelvic fracture.
Intraperitoneal: urine into abdominal cavity, commonly from a dome rupture of a full bladder.
Iatrogenic: during gynecologic, caesarean or endoscopic urological procedures.

coreShorts.q: State symptoms and diagnosis of bladder trauma.
a: Gross haematuria, suprapubic pain, inability to urinate or weak/strained stream, abdominal tenderness and distention.
Diagnosis: CT cystogram or conventional X-ray cystography.

coreShorts.q: Compare treatment of extraperitoneal and intraperitoneal bladder rupture.
a: Extraperitoneal: usually catheter drainage for 10–14 days.
Intraperitoneal: almost always surgical repair, laparoscopic or open.

coreShorts.q: Differentiate posterior and anterior urethral injuries.
a: Posterior: primarily associated with pelvic fractures after high-impact accidents.
Anterior: usually straddle injury or direct penile trauma.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate the classic signs and diagnosis of urethral trauma.
a: Blood at the meatus.
Inability to void.
Perineal ecchymosis.
Floating prostate on examination.
Diagnosis: retrograde urethrogram showing possible contrast extravasation.

coreShorts.q: Outline management and complications of urethral trauma.
a: Initial urinary diversion: suprapubic tube.
Partial tears: conservative management.
Complete injuries: urethroplasty, often delayed 3–6 months.
Complications: urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.

coreShorts.q: Describe clinical assessment and imaging of scrotal trauma.
a: Intense pain, nausea/vomiting, bruising, edema and possible haematuria.
High-resolution scrotal ultrasound with Doppler is the gold standard.
The cremasteric reflex may be lost; swelling may obscure examination.

coreShorts.q: Enumerate types of scrotal/testicular injury.
a: Testicular rupture.
Testicular fracture.
Intratesticular or extratesticular hematoma.
Testicular dislocation.
Traumatic torsion.

coreShorts.q: Differentiate testicular rupture and testicular fracture.
a: Rupture: tunica-albuginea tear with extrusion of tubules.
Fracture: parenchymal disruption without a complete tunica-albuginea tear.

coreShorts.q: Outline management and complications of scrotal trauma.
a: Mild contusions: bed rest, scrotal elevation/support, ice packs and NSAID analgesia.
Explore suspected rupture, significant hematocele, persistent severe symptoms and penetrating injury.
Complications: atrophy, chronic pain, infertility, psychological impact and infection of hematoma.

detailedShorts.q: What makes a urological emergency an emergency?
detailedShorts.a: It requires immediate intervention to prevent permanent organ damage or life-threatening complications.

detailedShorts.q: Name the six common emergencies listed before the trauma section.
detailedShorts.a: Acute urinary retention, testicular torsion, priapism, penile fracture, paraphimosis and Fournier gangrene.

detailedShorts.q: What is the first-line treatment of acute urinary retention?
detailedShorts.a: Immediate bladder catheterization and decompression.

detailedShorts.q: Name the catheter routes mentioned for acute retention.
detailedShorts.a: Indwelling Foley urethral catheter or suprapubic catheter.

detailedShorts.q: State four causes of acute urinary retention.
detailedShorts.a: BPH, urethral stricture, medications and neurological disorders.

detailedShorts.q: What happens anatomically in testicular torsion?
detailedShorts.a: The spermatic cord twists and cuts off testicular blood supply.

detailedShorts.q: What Doppler finding supports testicular torsion?
detailedShorts.a: Reduced blood flow to the affected testis.

detailedShorts.q: What is the ideal salvage time for testicular torsion?
detailedShorts.a: Detorsion and orchiopexy within 6 hours.

detailedShorts.q: What is the prognosis after 24 hours of torsion?
detailedShorts.a: The testis can rarely be saved.

detailedShorts.q: What is the role of manual detorsion?
detailedShorts.a: It may be attempted but must not delay surgery.

detailedShorts.q: Define bell-clapper deformity.
detailedShorts.a: The testis hangs freely in the scrotum, allowing it to twist.

detailedShorts.q: What duration defines priapism in the lecture?
detailedShorts.a: More than 4 hours.

detailedShorts.q: Name the two types of priapism.
detailedShorts.a: Ischemic low-flow and non-ischemic high-flow.

detailedShorts.q: What is the sequence of treatment for ischemic priapism?
detailedShorts.a: Cavernosal aspiration followed by intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection such as phenylephrine.

detailedShorts.q: What simple measures are mentioned for non-ischemic priapism?
detailedShorts.a: Observation and ice packs with urological consultation.

detailedShorts.q: Which penile layer ruptures in penile fracture?
detailedShorts.a: Tunica albuginea.

detailedShorts.q: What is rapid detumescence?
detailedShorts.a: Immediate loss of erection after the fracture event.

detailedShorts.q: What is eggplant deformity?
detailedShorts.a: Dark-purple bruising/hematoma with rapid penile swelling.

detailedShorts.q: Which sign suggests urethral involvement in penile fracture?
detailedShorts.a: Urethral bleeding/blood at the tip of the penis.

detailedShorts.q: Name three late complications of delayed penile-fracture treatment.
detailedShorts.a: Penile curvature, erectile dysfunction and painful intercourse.

detailedShorts.q: Define phimosis.
detailedShorts.a: Inability to retract the prepuce behind the glans.

detailedShorts.q: Define paraphimosis.
detailedShorts.a: A retracted prepuce cannot return to its original position.

detailedShorts.q: What operative release is used after failed manual reduction of paraphimosis?
detailedShorts.a: Dorsal slit incision.

detailedShorts.q: Which tissues are involved in Fournier gangrene?
detailedShorts.a: Perineum, scrotum and genitalia.

detailedShorts.q: Which organisms must empiric antibiotics cover in Fournier gangrene?
detailedShorts.a: Gram-positive, gram-negative and anaerobic organisms.

detailedShorts.q: What is the essential surgical step in Fournier gangrene?
detailedShorts.a: Immediate aggressive debridement of necrotic tissue.

detailedShorts.q: List the five traumatic urological emergency groups.
detailedShorts.a: Renal, ureteral, bladder, urethral and scrotal trauma.

detailedShorts.q: Classify trauma by basic mechanism.
detailedShorts.a: Blunt and penetrating injury.

detailedShorts.q: What is the most common symptom of renal trauma?
detailedShorts.a: Haematuria.

detailedShorts.q: What imaging assesses renal injury grade?
detailedShorts.a: CT scan with angiography using the AAST scale.

detailedShorts.q: What treatment is used for active renal bleeding?
detailedShorts.a: Angioembolization.

detailedShorts.q: Name two delayed renal-trauma complications.
detailedShorts.a: Hypertension and urinoma.

detailedShorts.q: What is the commonest cause of ureteral trauma?
detailedShorts.a: Iatrogenic injury, especially gynecologic surgery such as hysterectomy.

detailedShorts.q: What percentage of ureteral injuries are often diagnosed postoperatively in the lecture?
Which CT protocol is important in suspected ureteral injury?
detailedShorts.a: CT urography with contrast and delayed imaging.

detailedShorts.q: What stent is used for minor ureteral injury?
detailedShorts.a: JJ stent.

detailedShorts.q: Name two reconstructive operations for significant ureteral injury.
detailedShorts.a: Ureteroureterostomy and ureteroneocystostomy.

detailedShorts.q: What diversion may be used for ureteral trauma?
detailedShorts.a: Percutaneous nephrostomy.

detailedShorts.q: Where does urine leak in extraperitoneal bladder rupture?
detailedShorts.a: Into pelvic tissues.

detailedShorts.q: Where does urine leak in intraperitoneal bladder rupture?
detailedShorts.a: Into the abdominal cavity.

detailedShorts.q: Which bladder site commonly ruptures intraperitoneally?
detailedShorts.a: The bladder dome when the bladder is full.

detailedShorts.q: What is the standard diagnostic test for bladder trauma?
detailedShorts.a: CT cystogram or conventional X-ray cystography.

detailedShorts.q: How long is catheter drainage commonly used for extraperitoneal rupture?
detailedShorts.a: 10–14 days.

detailedShorts.q: What trauma is classically linked to posterior urethral injury?
detailedShorts.a: Pelvic fracture from high-impact trauma.

detailedShorts.q: What trauma is classically linked to anterior urethral injury?
detailedShorts.a: Straddle injury or direct penile trauma.

detailedShorts.q: What is the standard imaging for suspected urethral injury?
detailedShorts.a: Retrograde urethrogram.

detailedShorts.q: What is the preferred initial diversion in urethral trauma?
detailedShorts.a: Suprapubic tube insertion.

detailedShorts.q: When is urethroplasty often performed for complete injury?
detailedShorts.a: After a delay of 3–6 months.

detailedShorts.q: What is the gold-standard imaging for scrotal trauma?
detailedShorts.a: High-resolution scrotal ultrasound with Doppler.

detailedShorts.q: Define testicular rupture.
detailedShorts.a: Tunica-albuginea tear with extrusion of testicular tubules.

detailedShorts.q: Define testicular fracture.
detailedShorts.a: Disruption of testicular parenchyma without a full tunica-albuginea tear.

detailedShorts.q: How are mild scrotal contusions managed?
detailedShorts.a: Bed rest, scrotal support/elevation, ice packs and NSAID analgesia.

detailedShorts.q: State indications for scrotal exploration from the lecture.
detailedShorts.a: Suspected rupture, significant hematocele, persistent severe symptoms and penetrating injury.

imageQuestions.title: Bell-Clapper Deformity and Torsion
imageQuestions.prompt: The figure compares a normal testis, a freely mobile testis and a twisted testis.
questions: Identify the emergency shown.
Name the predisposing deformity.
State the typical age group and urgent management.
answer: Testicular torsion.
Bell-clapper deformity, where the testis hangs freely and can twist.
Most common in adolescents during rapid growth. Urgent surgical detorsion and orchiopexy within 6 hours; manual detorsion must not delay surgery.

Which structure is torn?
State definitive management.

imageQuestions.title: Paraphimosis and Dorsal Slit
imageQuestions.prompt: The slide shows a constricting ring, manual compression/reduction and a dorsal-slit incision.
questions: Identify the condition.
Why is it urgent?
Describe the illustrated rescue procedure.
answer: Paraphimosis.
Delay can cause glans gangrene.
If manual repositioning fails, a dorsal-slit incision releases the constricting ring.

imageQuestions.title: Fournier's Gangrene
imageQuestions.prompt: The clinical photograph shows extensive dark necrotic genital tissue.
questions: Identify the diagnosis.
Define it.
State immediate management.
answer: Fournier's gangrene.
Rapidly progressing necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, scrotum and genitalia.
Immediate aggressive debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation and septic-shock/ICU support.

imageQuestions.title: AAST Renal Trauma Chart
imageQuestions.prompt: The chart grades renal injury from contusion to shattered kidney/pedicle avulsion.
questions: Name the grading system.
Differentiate grades 1–3.
State the key grade 4 and grade 5 patterns.
answer: AAST (American Association for the Surgery of Trauma) renal injury grading.

Grade 1: contusion/non-expanding subcapsular hematoma, no laceration. Grade 2: non-expanding perirenal hematoma or cortical laceration <1 cm without extravasation. Grade 3: cortical laceration >1 cm without extravasation.
Grade 4: collecting-system laceration or segmental vascular injury with contained hematoma/partial laceration/thrombosis. Grade 5: shattered kidney or renal-pedicle avulsion.

imageQuestions.title: Traumatic Bladder Injury Mechanisms
imageQuestions.prompt: The diagram illustrates blunt, penetrating and iatrogenic bladder injuries.
questions: Enumerate the mechanisms shown.
Classify bladder rupture by urine-leak location.
State the standard diagnostic study.
answer: Blunt, penetrating and iatrogenic injuries.
Extraperitoneal leakage into pelvic tissues; intraperitoneal leakage into the abdominal cavity.
CT cystogram or conventional cystography.

imageQuestions.title: Anterior and Posterior Urethra
imageQuestions.prompt: The schematic labels penile/bulbar and membranous/prostatic urethral segments.
questions: Which segments form the anterior and posterior urethra in the diagram?
Which trauma mechanism is typical for each injury group?
answer: Anterior urethra: penile and bulbar segments. Posterior urethra: membranous and prostatic segments.
Anterior injury: straddle/direct penile trauma. Posterior injury: pelvic fracture after high-impact trauma.

imageQuestions.title: Straddle Injury Mechanism
imageQuestions.prompt: The illustration shows a cyclist falling onto a hard bar.
questions: Which urethral injury is suggested?
List the classic signs.
State the diagnostic test.
answer: Anterior urethral injury.
Blood at meatus, inability to void and perineal ecchymosis.
Retrograde urethrogram.

imageQuestions.title: Pelvic-Fracture Urethral Injury
imageQuestions.prompt: The diagram shows disruption around the posterior urethra and upward displacement of the prostate.
questions: Identify the injury group.
Name the classic examination sign suggested.
State initial urinary diversion.
answer: Posterior urethral injury associated with pelvic fracture.
Floating prostate.
Suprapubic tube insertion.

imageQuestions.title: Retrograde Urethrogram
imageQuestions.prompt: The radiographs show contrast outlining the urethra with abnormal extravasation/stricture patterns.
questions: Name the investigation.
When is it indicated in this lecture?
What abnormality may it show?
State key complications of urethral injury.
answer: Retrograde urethrogram (RGU).
Suspected urethral injury, especially blood at the meatus or inability to void after pelvic/straddle trauma.
Contrast extravasation; later images may demonstrate urethral stricture.
Stricture, erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.
